name: Aspirin mask

lead: The aspirin mask is a home paste made from crushed aspirin tablets, applied to the face by people who want clearer, less red skin and fewer breakouts.

The reasoning runs through salicylic acid, a common acne ingredient: aspirin is acetylsalicylic acid and is broken down to salicylic acid in the body. Users expect a similar pore-clearing, calming effect on the skin. Salicylic acid itself is studied for acne; no studies of the aspirin mask were found.

paras: People mix crushed tablets with water or another base into a paste, leave it on for a short time as a wash-off mask, and rinse. It is used as an occasional spot or whole-face treatment alongside a normal cleanser and moisturizer. Users usually look for a change in redness within hours and in breakouts over repeated uses.

The documented warnings about aspirin concern oral use, such as stomach irritation and bleeding risk and avoidance by people with aspirin allergy. Effects of a topical aspirin paste are not described in the sources reviewed, so irritation on the face is possible but not characterised. People allergic to aspirin or salicylates have reason to avoid it.

wikipedia.title: List of King of Mask Singer episodes (2020)

lead: An aspirin mask is a home paste made by crushing aspirin tablets, applied to the face, mainly for acne and redness. Proponents note that aspirin is related to salicylic acid, a common acne ingredient.
Aspirin is acetylsalicylic acid and is broken down in the body to salicylic acid [1]. Wikipedia's aspirin article does not discuss acne use, and no studies of aspirin masks were found.

paras: Aspirin is produced by acetylating salicylic acid, and it is readily converted to salicylic acid in the body [1]. Wikipedia mentions topical aspirin only in the context of possible effectiveness for some neuropathic pain [1].

Oral aspirin is associated with stomach upset, ulcers, bleeding and worsening asthma, and is not recommended in late pregnancy or for children with viral infections because of Reye syndrome [1]. These effects relate to oral use; the sources do not describe topical masks.
